original_value:
Objects obscured by occluders are considered lost in the images acquired by conventional camera systems, prohibiting both visualization and understanding of such hidden objects. Non-line-of-sight methods (NLOS) aim at recovering information about hidden scenes, which could help make medical imaging less invasive, improve the safety of autonomous vehicles, and potentially enable capturing unprecedented high-definition RGB-D data sets that include geometry beyond the directly visible parts. Recent NLOS methods have demonstrated scene recovery from time-resolved pulse-illuminated measurements encoding occluded objects as faint indirect reflections. Unfortunately, these systems are fundamentally limited by the quartic intensity fall-off for diffuse scenes. With laser illumination limited by eye-safety limits, recovery algorithms must tackle this challenge by incorporating scene priors. However, existing NLOS reconstruction algorithms do not facilitate learning scene priors. Even if they did, datasets that allow for such supervision do not exist, and successful encoder-decoder networks and generative adversarial networks fail for real-world NLOS data. In this work, we close this gap by learning hidden scene feature representations tailored to both reconstruction and recognition tasks such as classification or object detection, while still relying on physical models at the feature level. We
            overcome the lack of real training data
            with a generalizable architecture that can be trained in simulation. We learn the differentiable scene representation jointly with the reconstruction task using a differentiable transient renderer in the objective, and demonstrate that it
            generalizes to unseen classes and unseen real-world scenes
            , unlike existing encoder-decoder architectures and generative adversarial networks. The proposed method allows for
            end-to-end training for different NLOS tasks
            , such as image reconstruction, classification, and object detection, while being memory-efficient and running at real-time rates. We demonstrate
            hidden view synthesis, RGB-D reconstruction, classification, and object detection
            in the hidden scene in an end-to-end fashion.

result.paraphrase: Conventional camera systems treat objects blocked by occluders as lost, making both visualization and interpretation of hidden objects impossible. Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) methods seek to recover information about unseen scenes, with potential to make medical imaging less invasive, improve autonomous vehicle safety, and ultimately enable unprecedented high-definition RGB-D datasets that capture geometry beyond directly visible regions. Recent NLOS approaches have shown scene recovery from time-resolved, pulse-illuminated measurements that encode occluded objects as faint indirect reflections. However, these systems are fundamentally constrained by quartic intensity fall-off in diffuse scenes. Because laser illumination is limited by eye-safety constraints, recovery algorithms must address this challenge by incorporating scene priors. Existing NLOS reconstruction methods, however, do not support learning such priors. Even if they did, suitable supervised datasets do not exist, and effective encoder-decoder networks and generative adversarial networks fail on real-world NLOS data. In this work, we bridge this gap by learning hidden-scene feature representations designed for both reconstruction and recognition tasks such as classification and object detection, while still using physical models at the feature level. We address the absence of real training data with a generalizable architecture that can be trained in simulation. Using a differentiable transient renderer in the objective, we learn the differentiable scene representation jointly with reconstruction, and show that it generalizes to unseen classes and unseen real-world scenes, unlike existing encoder-decoder architectures and GANs. The proposed method enables end-to-end training across different NLOS tasks, including image reconstruction, classification, and object detection, while remaining memory-efficient and operating in real time. We demonstrate end-to-end hidden view synthesis, RGB-D reconstruction, classification, and object detection in the hidden scene.
